idiom_name: abstract framework class with virtual hook methods (Qt-style event dispatch)
implementation_notes: The classic C++ form: an abstract base class declares the hook methods, and the framework's loop or dispatcher owns main() and calls them on your override at the moment it chooses. Qt is the canonical example - QCoreApplication::exec() runs the event loop and delivers each QEvent to QObject::event(), which dispatches to virtual handlers such as paintEvent() - and that same structure is what you hand-write for a framework of your own. Prefer it when the extension must be a framework-registered object anyway or when hooks need protected framework state; prefer callback registration when extensions should not inherit from the framework.
pitfalls: A virtual hook called from the framework's constructor runs before your override is fully initialised; never rely on derived state in a hook invoked during construction.
Forgetting to call the base implementation (or to forward unhandled events) silently drops default framework behaviour.

variants.name: Callback registration with std::function
variants.idiom_name: std::function/lambda handlers registered with a dispatcher
variants.implementation_notes: C++11 makes callbacks first-class: the dispatcher stores std::function objects (lambdas, bind expressions or function pointers) and invokes them, so extensions no longer have to inherit from the framework. This replaces the virtual-hook base class with registration plus a callable, which suits plugins and callbacks that must be composed, replaced or configured at runtime. Keep the virtual-hook form when the hook set is fixed and hot, because std::function type-erases and may allocate for large captures.
pitfalls: Dangling captures: a lambda capturing a local or a raw this keeps working only as long as the referenced object lives, and the dispatcher must not outlive it.
std::function copies the callable and may allocate for large captures, so per-event registration on a hot path is measurably slower than a virtual call.

variants.name: Suspend/resume handlers with C++20 coroutines
variants.idiom_name: co_await suspension points resumed by the framework's executor
variants.implementation_notes: With C++20 coroutines the framework's completion path resumes your coroutine at the co_await suspension point, so the inversion becomes a suspending function instead of a callback chain while the executor still decides when your code continues. This replaces the completion-handler pyramid with ordinary sequential code without moving control to the application. Use it when the toolchain is C++20 and the framework exposes an awaiter interface; the virtual-hook and std::function forms stay simpler for synchronous callbacks.
pitfalls: A coroutine must own or outlive everything it references across a suspension point; detached spawns are the coroutine-era version of the dangling-callback bug.
Exception and cancellation semantics cross the suspension boundary, so the framework's resume path must be able to deliver both to the suspended frame.
